title: The Eton Park Lunch: Two Hours in the Secretary’s Calendar, Eight Days After He Said the GSEs Would Stay Shareholder-Owned
participants: Henry M. Paulson, Jr. (Secretary of the Treasury)
Federal Reserve Bank of New York

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: Nothing in the documents read here records a skim, and the dossier does not assert one. What the documents record is an opportunity and its shape: on 21 July 2008, between 12:00 and 2:00 PM, the Secretary of the Treasury kept a "Lunch Roundtable with Hedge Fund and Private Equity Firm Managers" at Eton Park Capital Management, 823 Third Avenue, followed that evening by dinner at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York.
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: The public position eight days earlier was the opposite of what was coming. On 13 July 2008 the Secretary announced that Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac "must continue to do so in their current form as shareholder-owned companies", and set out a three-part plan — a temporary credit line, temporary authority to purchase equity, and a consultative role for the Federal Reserve. Seven weeks later both companies were in conservatorship. Anyone who learned in between that the second outcome was being contemplated held something the market did not.
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: The fog is in the record itself, and it is not an accident of this dossier. Treasury’s own note on these calendars says they "do not include unplanned or impromptu items" and that "certain limited aspects of the Secretary’s calendars have been reformatted to protect sensitive information"; several entries on the same page are blacked out under the personal-privacy exemption. The calendar fixes the meeting, the place and the two hours. It names no attendee and records not one word that was said. No transcript, minute, note or testimony of that lunch was found in any source opened for this dossier.
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: The statutory machinery arrived nine days after the lunch. The Housing and Economic Recovery Act, signed 30 July 2008, gave the Secretary authority to purchase the GSEs’ obligations and securities "on such terms and conditions as the Secretary may determine and in such amounts as the Secretary may determine", subject to an emergency determination that the action was needed to provide stability, prevent disruption in mortgage finance and protect the taxpayer, and created the Federal Housing Finance Agency with its conservatorship powers. On 6 September the two boards consented; on 7 September the conservatorships were announced over $5.4 trillion of guaranteed securities and debt.
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: There was no inquiry to whitewash. No investigation of the lunch is recorded in any document read here, and no agency made a finding about it. What exists instead is a precision that the popular retelling loses: the FHFA Director’s statement of 7 September says that "the common stock and preferred stock dividends will be eliminated" while "the common and all preferred stocks will continue to remain outstanding". The equity was not formally extinguished. Anyone who shorted it on a belief that it would be was right about the direction and wrong about the mechanism.

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: The implicit federal guarantee behind the two housing enterprises, and a Treasury convention of private briefing sessions with market participants that leaves a calendar line and nothing else.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: Section 1117 of HERA — an open-ended, Secretary-determined purchase authority over the obligations of two private corporations — together with FHFA conservatorship, the pairing that made the September action possible and that later carried the net worth sweep.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: The asymmetry recirculates through the diary rather than through a payment. The Secretary’s public statement and his private calendar are both preserved; the content that would connect them is preserved nowhere, so the episode can neither be proved nor cleared, and is argued on both sides from the same two documents.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: That the Treasury Secretary told a room of former Goldman Sachs colleagues at a hedge fund in July 2008 that Fannie and Freddie would be put into conservatorship and their common and preferred stock wiped out, handing them weeks to position themselves while he told the public the opposite.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: The account of what was said rests on a single magazine report built on anonymous attendees, and no document read for this dossier corroborates any part of it: not an attendee list, not a note, not a transcript, not a finding by any agency. Two of its details are also wrong against the primary record. The equity was not wiped out as a formal matter — FHFA’s own announcement of 7 September 2008 eliminated the dividends but left "the common and all preferred stocks ... outstanding". And the existence of a rescue plan was not secret on 21 July: the Secretary had announced a three-part plan publicly on 13 July, and the legislation carrying the purchase authority was then before Congress and was signed nine days after the lunch. What a listener could have learned at that table was not that something was coming, but which of the announced options was being favoured — a narrower advantage than the story describes, and one no document read here shows anyone receiving.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: The Secretary of the Treasury’s own official calendar for July 2008 records a two-hour "Lunch Roundtable with Hedge Fund and Private Equity Firm Managers" at Eton Park Capital Management, 823 Third Avenue, on Monday 21 July 2008. Eight days earlier he had said publicly that the two enterprises "must continue to do so in their current form as shareholder-owned companies". Nine days afterwards the Housing and Economic Recovery Act gave him authority to buy their obligations and securities in amounts and on terms of his own determining, and created the regulator that would hold them. Seven weeks afterwards the boards of both consented to conservatorship over $5.4 trillion of guaranteed MBS and debt, their dividends eliminated and their shares left outstanding. What was said in those two hours is not in the record, and this dossier does not supply it.

citations.title: U.S. Department of the Treasury, Calendar of Secretary Henry M. Paulson, Jr., July 2008 (Electronic Reading Room, "Calendars and Travel of the Secretary")
citations.quoteOrFact: A 60-page scan with no text layer; downloaded and read page by page in a browser. The page covering 20–22 July 2008 records, for Monday 21 July, an entry running 12:00 PM to 2:00 PM: "Lunch Roundtable with Hedge Fund and Private Equity Firm Managers, Eton Park Capital Management, Boardroom 823 3rd Avenue". The same day's entries include a press pre-brief at the Waldorf Astoria, an on-the-record interview with New York Times business reporters, a Business Week editorial board meeting, a live CNBC interview, and, at 6:45 PM, "Dinner at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York". Several entries on the same page are blacked out under the FOIA personal-privacy exemption, marked "(b) (6)". WHAT THIS DOCUMENT DOES NOT SHOW: it records a meeting, a place, a two-hour window and a description of who was present in general terms. It does not name any attendee, record any agenda, or record a word of what was said. Treasury's own page publishing these calendars states that they "reflect scheduled meetings, calls, and events that occurred", that they "do not include unplanned or impromptu items", and that "certain limited aspects of the Secretary's calendars have been reformatted to protect sensitive information."

citations.title: U.S. Department of the Treasury, "Paulson Announces GSE Initiatives", press release HP-1079, 13 July 2008
citations.quoteOrFact: Read in full on Treasury's own site (archived content). Eight days before the Eton Park lunch, the Secretary's public position was: "Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac play a central role in our housing finance system and must continue to do so in their current form as shareholder-owned companies." The statement announces "a three-part plan for immediate action" developed in consultation with the Federal Reserve, OFHEO, the SEC, congressional leaders of both parties and the two companies: first, "a temporary increase in the line of credit the GSEs have with Treasury"; second, "temporary authority for Treasury to purchase equity in either of the two GSEs if needed"; third, strengthening the GSE regulatory reform legislation "currently moving through Congress" by giving the Federal Reserve "a consultative role in the new GSE regulator's process for setting capital requirements and other prudential standards." The release says nothing about conservatorship and nothing about the treatment of common or preferred shareholders.

citations.title: Housing and Economic Recovery Act of 2008, Pub. L. 110-289, 122 STAT. 2654 (30 July 2008) — section 1117, Temporary Authority for Purchase of Obligations of Regulated Entities by Secretary of Treasury
citations.quoteOrFact: Downloaded from govinfo and read as extracted text. Enacted 30 July 2008, nine days after the Eton Park lunch. Section 1117 adds to the Fannie Mae charter act a new subsection (g) under which "the Secretary of the Treasury is authorized to purchase any obligations and other securities issued by the corporation under any section of this Act, on such terms and conditions as the Secretary may determine and in such amounts as the Secretary may determine", with parallel provisions for Freddie Mac and the Federal Home Loan Banks. The authority carries an "EMERGENCY DETERMINATION REQUIRED": in connection with any use of it the Secretary "must determine that such actions are necessary to — (i) provide stability to the financial markets; (ii) prevent disruptions in the availability of mortgage finance; and (iii) protect the taxpayer." It expressly does not permit the Secretary, without the corporation's agreement, "to engage in open market purchases of the common securities of the corporation". The same Act created the Federal Housing Finance Agency and its conservatorship and receivership powers over the regulated entities.

citations.title: Federal Housing Finance Agency, "Statement of FHFA Director James B. Lockhart at News Conference Announcing Conservatorship of Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac", 7 September 2008
citations.quoteOrFact: Read on FHFA's own site. The statement, dated 7 September 2008, puts the Enterprises' obligations at "$5.4 trillion of guaranteed mortgage-backed securities (MBS) and debt outstanding" and gives as the ground for action that "the companies cannot continue to operate safely and soundly and fulfill their critical public mission". On governance: "FHFA will assume the power of the Board and management", and "The Boards of both companies consented yesterday to the conservatorship" — that is, on 6 September 2008. On the equity, the statement is precise and is not what the popular account of the episode says: "the common stock and preferred stock dividends will be eliminated", but "the common and all preferred stocks will continue to remain outstanding", with subordinated debt payments continuing. The sitting chief executives were replaced, by Herb Allison at Fannie Mae and David Moffett at Freddie Mac.
